teaser: A wild animal on a blank page, with a window shining in its eye.
review_notes:
Window reflection in the hare's eye: visible in our image as small bright panes in the near eye (x 0.60, y 0.53); standard observation.
Whether Dürer worked from a live animal, a dead one, or both is unknown; presented as open.
Watercolor and gouache on paper, about 25 x 23 cm.
Albertina display policy (shown only for short periods every few years, then years of rest in the dark; a facsimile shown otherwise): check current wording.
Provenance: Imhoff family in Nuremberg, bought by Emperor Rudolf II in 1588, later to Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen, founder of the Albertina.
Hans Hoffmann's hare copies and variations, late 16th century.
Ottmar Hörl, 'Das grosse Hasenstück', Nuremberg main market square, 2003: about 7,000 green plastic hares.
German title is 'Feldhase' (field hare); the word 'young' exists only in the English title.

lesson.text: Nothing in this picture should be possible. A hare is among the most nervous animals in Europe: it bolts at a footstep. Yet this one has held still long enough for a man to count its whiskers. It sits on bare paper, no grass, no field, no room. And still, shining in its dark eye, there is a piece of a building.
A window is hiding in this drawing. Where?

spots.title: The eye
spots.text: On the wet black of the pupil, a few bright patches divided by dark bars: the reflection of a window with its cross frame. The hare is looking into a room.

lesson.text: That speck of white paint moves the whole scene indoors, into Dürer's workshop in Nuremberg in 1502. How a hare got there is another matter. Did he keep a live one for a while? Sketch hares outdoors and finish from a dead animal? Nobody knows. The ears, turned two different ways as if still listening, argue for a living model.

You may travel to Vienna and not see it. The colors fade in light, so the Albertina brings the original out only for a few weeks every few years, then lets it rest in darkness. Most of the time visitors stand in front of a very good copy.

The sheet is small, about 25 by 23 centimeters (10 by 9 inches), so the animal is well under life-size. Dürer used watercolor, pigment thinned with water so the paper shows through, and gouache, a similar paint made opaque with white so it covers what lies beneath. The first is for softness, the second for sharp light lines.

He worked from blurry to sharp. First, loose washes of brown for the general shape and its shadows. Then hundreds of short strokes with a fine brush, dark ones, then pale ones on top. The trick is that fur is never one thing. It changes length, color and direction every few centimeters.

lesson.title: Four kinds of fur
lesson.text: Travel from tail to nose and watch the brush change its habits.

spots.title: The haunch
spots.text: On the rump, thick tufts curl in rows and turn blue-gray in the shadow. The strokes are broad and soft: this is the dense coat that keeps the animal warm.

spots.title: The flank
spots.text: Lower down the hair goes pale, almost white, and lies in long loose strands. Dürer lets opaque white paint do the work here.

spots.title: The ears
spots.text: Short, flat hair, darker at the tip. One ear tilts back and shows its pale inner edge, the other stands straight up. They are not a matching pair.

spots.title: The whiskers
spots.text: Each whisker is a single stroke, laid in one unbroken sweep over the finished fur and out across the bare paper. One wobble and the sheet is spoiled.

lesson.text: Patience alone does not explain the result. Dürer never paints every hair. He paints enough of them, in the right directions, for your eye to supply the rest. And around the animal he adds one thing only: a gray shadow on the right, which tells you the light comes from the left and gives the hare a floor to sit on.
Before Dürer, an animal was a detail in somebody else's story. Here a hare is the whole subject, looked at as carefully as a prince.

Under the paws he wrote the year and his monogram, a D standing inside a large A. Artists rarely signed studies kept for their own use. Putting his mark on this sheet says that he considered it finished, a work in its own right, with nothing sacred or noble in it but attention.

Collectors agreed with him early. In 1588, sixty years after Dürer's death, Emperor Rudolf II, a ruler obsessed with art and natural curiosities, bought the hare from a Nuremberg family for his collection in Prague.

Around the same time a wave of imitation swept Germany. The painter Hans Hoffmann made a small career of Dürer hares: copies, hares in the forest, hares among flowers. More than a dozen old versions survive, some with a forged AD. It may be the most copied animal in art.
In 2003 the artist Ottmar Hörl covered Nuremberg's main square with about 7,000 green plastic hares, all modeled on this one. Dürer's hometown had turned his study into a mascot.
Return to the two ears. One relaxed, one on alert. Five centuries, an emperor, thousands of copies, and the animal on the sheet is still deciding whether to stay or run.

quiz.question: What is reflected in the hare's eye?
options: A window with its cross frame
quiz.explanation: The bright patches divided by bars are a workshop window.

quiz.question: What is gouache?
options: Water-based paint made opaque with white
quiz.explanation: It covers what lies beneath, which makes it good for sharp light lines.

quiz.question: What is the only thing Dürer painted around the animal?
quiz.explanation: The shadow on the right gives the hare a floor and shows where the light comes from.

quiz.question: Why do visitors to the Albertina usually see a copy?
options: The colors fade in light, so the original is rarely shown
The original is on permanent loan to Nuremberg
quiz.explanation: The sheet is light-sensitive and rests in darkness most of the time.

quiz.question: How did Dürer begin the fur?
options: With loose brown washes for shape and shadow
quiz.explanation: He went from blurry washes to fine strokes, and the whiskers came last.

facts.text: Dürer signed and dated the sheet.
facts.explanation: The year 1502 and his AD monogram sit below the paws.

facts.text: The hare's two ears are in exactly the same position.
facts.explanation: One tilts back and the other stands upright.

facts.text: The hare is painted in oil on a wooden panel.
facts.explanation: It is watercolor and gouache on paper.
